headline: Wolfram and Bach Test Whether Scale Unlocks Machine Consciousness
lede: On May 29, 2025, the California Institute for Machine Consciousness brings Stephen Wolfram and Joscha Bach together at San Francisco's Internet Archive for an evening framed around a single question: what would larger cognitive capacity actually produce? The pairing is deliberate — both thinkers have built elaborate, ground-up accounts of mind that challenge the reigning engineering assumption that capability is simply a function of compute.
body:
The question *What if we had Bigger Brains?* arrives at an opportune moment. The dominant working hypothesis in AI development holds that intelligence scales with parameters, data, and compute — a framework that has produced striking results but says little about whether any of it constitutes understanding or experience. The California Institute for Machine Consciousness (CIMC) runs salons at the intersection of AI and philosophy of mind, and this event places two of the more systematic thinkers on that boundary in the same room.

**Stephen Wolfram**, founder of Wolfram Research and creator of *Mathematica*, has for several years been pursuing the Wolfram Physics Project — an attempt to derive all of physical law from a single evolving *hypergraph*, a network of abstract nodes whose update rules generate space, time, and matter as emergent phenomena. In that picture a brain is not categorically special; it is a computational process embedded in the same underlying structure as everything else. Whether making it "bigger" changes what it *is*, rather than merely what it can do, is exactly the kind of question his framework was built to probe.

Joscha Bach, a cognitive scientist and AI researcher, offers a complementary but distinct account. His *computational theory of mind* holds that consciousness is the brain's running self-simulation — a compressed internal model of the system itself that enables flexible, context-sensitive behavior. On this view what matters is not the sheer scale of a system but the architecture of its self-model: how it represents its own representations, and whether that loop closes in a way that constitutes genuine experience.

The silent reference point throughout is *the hard problem of consciousness*, philosopher David Chalmers's formulation of why any physical process should give rise to subjective experience at all. Scaling arguments — including those underlying today's large language models — largely bracket the question, treating mind as an input-output function. Both Wolfram and Bach have argued publicly that this evasion is insufficient. Convening at the Internet Archive, the nonprofit built on the premise that information persists beyond any particular substrate, the event implicitly asks whether substrate can ever be beside the point.

concepts.definition: The hypothesized property of an artificial system having genuine subjective experience — not merely behaving as if conscious, but possessing an inner life. Whether this is possible, and what physical or computational conditions would produce it, is the central question of the field.

An organization that hosts cross-disciplinary salons and events at the intersection of artificial intelligence, cognitive science, and philosophy of mind. Its focus is on whether machines can be genuinely conscious, not merely capable.

A term coined by philosopher David Chalmers for the puzzle of why physical processes give rise to subjective experience at all. It is 'hard' because it resists purely functional explanations: you can fully describe a brain's behavior without explaining why there is something it is like to be that brain.

Stephen Wolfram's ongoing research program proposing that the universe is generated by a single evolving hypergraph — a network of abstract nodes governed by update rules — from which space, time, and all physical laws emerge as emergent properties. It is a formal attempt to find the computational substrate beneath fundamental physics.

A generalization of a graph in which connections can link more than two nodes at once. In Wolfram's physics framework the universe is represented as an evolving hypergraph whose update rules generate all observable structure, including space and time.

The view that mental states and processes are fundamentally computational — that thinking, perceiving, and being conscious are forms of information processing that could in principle run on any suitable physical substrate, not exclusively biological neurons.

In Joscha Bach's account of mind, the brain's running model of itself: a compressed internal representation that tracks the system's own state and goals, enabling flexible goal-directed behavior. Bach argues this self-modeling loop is what gives rise to the experience of being a subject.

Neural networks trained on vast text corpora to predict and generate language. They process inputs as statistical patterns over tokens and produce outputs by sampling from learned probability distributions — a design that has proved surprisingly capable but that is agnostic about whether any form of inner experience is present.

books.title: A New Kind of Science
books.author: Stephen Wolfram
books.summary: Published in 2002, Wolfram's landmark and controversial work argues that simple computational rules — cellular automata — can generate the full complexity observed in nature. It proposed a paradigm shift: that computation, not traditional mathematics, is the right language for science. The book anticipated many ideas later formalized in the Wolfram Physics Project and remains a reference point in debates about whether the universe is fundamentally computational.
